## 3. Subjects and where their information comes from

Thirteen subjects: the five the data gate asks about and eight more. The twelfth is the user's requirement of section 1: the solution is chosen by a volume measured or estimated in writing, and not the largest by default. The thirteenth came from the article the user pasted (section 5).

| Subject | Sources |
| :- | :- |

Eight pages were not read on 2026-11-15, and each is marked where it stands. EUR-Lex answered two requests for the GDPR with an empty body, so its URL is the act's standard ELI form and nothing more. O'Reilly's page of Fundamentals of Data Engineering and the two pages of iso.org refused the request. DuckDB's two overview pages answered with a redirect alone, and the content behind it was not read. The pages of Confluent's and Looker's managed servers, in section 5, are known from a search result.

Some names differ from those the user was offered, and the document gives each as its page does:

- No guide named "Data Engineering Design Patterns" exists at Airflow or at Astronomer. The row of pipelines gives Airflow's Best Practices, Retry Policies and Backfill pages and Astronomer's "DAG writing best practices in Apache Airflow" in its place. Airflow's Best Practices page says a task gives the same outcome on every re-run and never uses the word "idempotent"; no page of Dagster on idempotency was found.
- DAMA UK's whitepaper on the six dimensions is for members alone. The six are read on the UK Government's page, which attributes them to DAMA UK.
- No general page on retention periods was found at CNPD. Its index of guidance was opened; the one document on retention read there, Deliberação n.º 1039/2017, covers call recordings alone.
- The second edition of Designing Data-Intensive Applications came out in March 2026.
- The Data Contract Specification is deprecated by its own page since version 3.1.0 of the Open Data Contract Standard, and supported in datacontract-cli "until the end of 2026". The user was offered both names; the standard comes first.
- Looker Studio's help answers as "Data Studio documentation". TimescaleDB's documentation answers under the Tiger Data name, and the extension keeps its own.
- Laravel's documentation answers at `laravel.com/framework/docs/`, where `laravel.com/docs/` redirects; the current version is 13.x. Prisma's unversioned documentation describes Prisma ORM 8, a release candidate, so the pages on query optimisation, on logging and on `migrate diff` are those of Prisma 7.
- Repositories that moved: SQLx to `transact-rs/sqlx`, SQLMesh to `SQLMesh/sqlmesh` (its README calls it a project of the Linux Foundation), Laravel Debugbar to `fruitcake/laravel-debugbar`, django-migration-linter to `David-Wobrock/django-migration-linter`. MariaDB's Knowledge Base redirects to `mariadb.com/docs`, and OWASP's CSV Injection page to `community.owasp.org`.
- Laravel Cloud's MySQL page is the one opened for its backups; no page for PostgreSQL was. Apache Avro's specification answers at a URL that holds the literal segment `++version++`; the newest version it lists is 1.12.0. MySQL's manual was read in version 8.4.

## 4. Tools the team runs

In an existing project the team runs what the project uses. Each tool runs only where the project's database and stack take it.

| Kind | Tools |
| :- | :- |
| Migrations and schema | Squawk (https://github.com/sbdchd/squawk); Atlas's `atlas migrate lint` (https://atlasgo.io/versioned/lint), which its page gives to Atlas Pro users alone from v0.38 on; SQLFluff (https://docs.sqlfluff.com/en/stable/); per stack: Laravel's `migrate --pretend` and `migrate:status` (https://laravel.com/framework/docs/migrations#running-migrations), Django's `sqlmigrate` and `makemigrations --check` (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.1/ref/django-admin/) and django-migration-linter (https://github.com/David-Wobrock/django-migration-linter), Alembic's `check` (https://alembic.sqlalchemy.org/en/latest/autogenerate.html#running-alembic-check-to-test-for-new-upgrade-operations), Prisma's `migrate diff`, documented for Prisma 7 alone (https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/v7/migrate/diff), Drizzle Kit (https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/kit-overview), golang-migrate's CLI (https://github.com/golang-migrate/migrate/tree/master/cmd/migrate), `sqlx migrate` (https://github.com/transact-rs/sqlx/blob/main/sqlx-cli/README.md); for large tables with no downtime: gh-ost (https://github.com/github/gh-ost), pt-online-schema-change (https://docs.percona.com/percona-toolkit/pt-online-schema-change.html), pgroll (https://github.com/xataio/pgroll), pg_repack (https://reorg.github.io/pg_repack/) |
| Queries and indexes | EXPLAIN with ANALYZE and BUFFERS, and the equivalents of MySQL, SQLite and MongoDB, on the pages section 3 gives for queries; pg_stat_statements (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/pgstatstatements.html) and auto_explain (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/auto-explain.html); MySQL's slow query log (https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/slow-query-log.html) with pt-query-digest (https://docs.percona.com/percona-toolkit/pt-query-digest.html); HypoPG (https://github.com/HypoPG/hypopg) and Dexter (https://github.com/ankane/dexter); pgBadger (https://github.com/darold/pgbadger) and PgHero (https://github.com/ankane/pghero); N+1 detectors per framework: Laravel's `Model::preventLazyLoading` (https://laravel.com/framework/docs/eloquent-relationships#preventing-lazy-loading), Telescope (https://laravel.com/framework/docs/telescope) and Debugbar (https://github.com/fruitcake/laravel-debugbar), django-debug-toolbar (https://django-debug-toolbar.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) and nplusone, whose last change is of 2022-11-25 (https://github.com/jmcarp/nplusone), Prisma's logging, documented for Prisma 7 (https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/v7/prisma-client/observability-and-logging/logging), Drizzle's (https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/goodies#logging) |
| Data quality | GX Core, a Python library with no command line of its own (https://github.com/great-expectations/great_expectations); Soda Core (https://github.com/sodadata/soda-core); `dbt test` (https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/commands/test), with dbt-expectations in Metaplane's maintained fork (https://github.com/metaplane/dbt-expectations) and dbt-utils (https://github.com/dbt-labs/dbt-utils); Pandera (https://pandera.readthedocs.io/en/stable/) and Pydantic (https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/get-started/) for Python; Zod (https://zod.dev/) and JSON Schema (https://json-schema.org/) for Node / TypeScript; datacontract-cli (https://cli.datacontract.com/); a comparison of tables before and after a load: reladiff, a fork of data-diff by one of its authors (https://github.com/erezsh/reladiff), since Datafold archived data-diff on 2024-05-17 (https://github.com/datafold/data-diff) |
| Pipelines and load | dbt (https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/local/install-dbt) and SQLMesh (https://github.com/SQLMesh/sqlmesh); Apache Airflow (https://airflow.apache.org/), Dagster (https://dagster.io/docs) and Prefect (https://www.prefect.io/docs), with the framework's queues and scheduler; dlt (https://dlthub.com/docs/intro), Airbyte (https://github.com/airbytehq/airbyte) and Meltano (https://github.com/meltano/meltano); DuckDB (https://duckdb.org/), Polars (https://pola.rs/) and pandas (https://pandas.pydata.org/); Debezium (https://debezium.io/documentation/reference/stable/index.html) and Kafka Connect (https://kafka.apache.org/44/kafka-connect/overview/); the database's bulk load, on the pages section 3 gives. In an existing project the team runs what the project uses; for a new one it chooses by the measured volume |
| Backups and restore | pg_dump (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/app-pgdump.html), pg_restore (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/app-pgrestore.html) and pg_basebackup (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/app-pgbasebackup.html); pgBackRest (https://github.com/pgbackrest/pgbackrest), Barman (https://github.com/EnterpriseDB/barman) and WAL-G (https://github.com/wal-g/wal-g); mysqldump, which its page says is not meant for fast or scalable backups of large data sets (https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/mysqldump.html), mydumper (https://github.com/mydumper/mydumper) and Percona XtraBackup (https://github.com/percona/percona-xtrabackup); mongodump (https://www.mongodb.com/docs/database-tools/mongodump/) and mongorestore (https://www.mongodb.com/docs/database-tools/mongorestore/); Litestream (https://github.com/benbjohnson/litestream) and SQLite's `.backup` (https://www.sqlite.org/cli.html); spatie/laravel-backup (https://github.com/spatie/laravel-backup); the backups of the provider the project uses, on the pages section 3 gives. A backup counts as proven only after a rehearsal restore, run in the project's own local or test environment and never over production |
| Volume and measuring | pgbench (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/pgbench.html) and sysbench (https://github.com/akopytov/sysbench); test data at the real size: the framework's factories and seeders, Faker for PHP (https://fakerphp.org/), for Python (https://faker.readthedocs.io/en/master/) and for JavaScript (https://fakerjs.dev/), PostgreSQL's `generate_series` (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-srf.html), DuckDB's TPC-H (https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/core_extensions/tpch.html) and TPC-DS (https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/core_extensions/tpcds.html) generators; EXPLAIN ANALYZE over that volume; hyperfine (https://github.com/sharkdp/hyperfine); the database's size statistics, `pg_total_relation_size` among them (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-admin.html); Grafana k6, for the load that arrives through the application (https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/). The solution is chosen by a volume measured or estimated in writing, and the measuring runs in the project's own local or test environment |
| Documentation, catalogue and lineage | `dbt docs` (https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/commands/cmd-docs); SQLGlot (https://github.com/tobymao/sqlglot) and SQLLineage (https://github.com/reata/sqllineage); OpenLineage's clients for Python (https://openlineage.io/docs/client/python/) and Java (https://openlineage.io/docs/client/java/) and Marquez (https://github.com/MarquezProject/marquez); tbls (https://github.com/k1LoW/tbls) and SchemaSpy (https://schemaspy.org/); datacontract-cli (https://cli.datacontract.com/); DataHub (https://github.com/datahub-project/datahub) and OpenMetadata (https://github.com/open-metadata/OpenMetadata), only where the project already uses them |

What the research found of the tools' state on 2026-11-15:

- Atlas's `atlas migrate lint` is given to Atlas Pro users alone from v0.38 on, by its own page: it is a paid command.
- Datafold archived data-diff on 2024-05-17, and its README names no replacement. reladiff, which the row gives, is a fork kept under the account of one person, one of data-diff's authors. The user was offered "data-diff, or what replaced it".
- calogica's dbt-expectations says it "is no longer actively supported"; Metaplane's fork calls itself the maintained one.
- Since 2026-09-16 "dbt v2.0 is GA" (https://docs.getdbt.com/blog/dbt-v2-is-ga): the Fusion engine carries the name "dbt", the default install is under a "dbt v2 license agreement", and the open-source runtime is "dbt-oss", Apache 2.0 (https://github.com/dbt-labs/dbt-core). "dbt Core" and "dbt Fusion" are no longer the documentation's names.
- GX Core has no command line of its own on the pages read. Soda Core's current version is 4, and 3 is legacy.
- `nplusone` was last changed on 2022-11-25, and sysbench on 2025-03-09 (release 1.0.20).
- Not checked: which anchor of PostgreSQL's page of administration functions holds the size functions, and Laravel's anchors beyond `eager-loading`, `database-transactions` and `running-migrations`.

## 5. MCP servers and skills

### The rules

1. The backend team's rule holds: an MCP server or a set of skills enters only when the tool's or the service's own team makes it. Nothing from the community, with the one exception of rule 6. A tool with no server of its own runs from the command line.
2. A database's or a provider's server is installed only where the project uses that database or provider, in read-only mode where the server has one, and the same team's skills are installed with it. A server with no read-only mode connects only to the project's own local or test database, or with an account that can only read. PostgreSQL and MySQL are reached through Google's MCP Toolbox for Databases or through the provider's server.
3. The server and the skills of a pipeline, quality, lineage or reporting tool are installed only where the project already uses the tool, in read-only mode where the server has one.
4. Skills with no server are installed with the tool.
5. Two sets of general skills are installed always. The six sets of skills that the security team's definition (`docs/specs/2026-11-15-security-team-design.md`, section 5) gives to every team's work apply to this team unchanged.
6. The user sent three links. One of them, a set of skills by one person, enters by the user's own choice and is the one exception to rule 1.
7. The team has eleven skills of its own, defined here and written in a later item.
8. A command that takes a token, a key, a password or a connection string is written with the variable's name or the page's placeholder and no value; a connection string is written with the page's placeholder or a local address with no credential.

Each row's second cell says where the server runs, whether it can write or act, how its read-only mode is switched on when it has one, and the label its publisher gives it when it gives one. A row whose server has no read-only mode, or whose page states none, says so: rule 2's local or test database holds for it. "Hosted" means the project's data leaves the machine.

### The team's own skills

Eleven skills, defined here and written in a later item. Each has its instructions, its references loaded only when they are needed, and every calculation in deterministic code. That form comes from the article the user pasted ("I Built A Digital Data Team In 30 Minutes", Reliable Data Engineering, 2026-01-18), which also names nine of the eleven. The article's figures (a return of 21,333%, the results of two teams) name no source and enter nowhere as facts.

| Skill | What it does |
| :- | :- |
| Data quality monitor | Reads incoming data against its expected schema, checks completeness, duplicates and outliers, and reports what failed |
| Pipeline generator | From the source data: infers the schema and the keys, writes the transformation and its tests, sized to the volume |
| Documentation and data dictionary generator | Writes a table's documentation from its schema and its data, and keeps it current when the schema changes |
| Query optimiser | Reads a slow query's plan and proposes the index or the rewrite, with the plan before and after |
| Lineage tracer | Follows a number from the report back to its origin through the queries and the transformations |
| Data test generator | Writes the tests a table's schema and data call for: uniqueness, ranges, consistency between fields |
| Source schema evolution handler | Compares the schema that arrived with the one expected, and says what was added, removed or renamed before a pipeline runs |
| Performance measuring | Times a query or a pipeline at a stated volume and keeps the measure to compare against |
| Data catalogue | Lists the datasets, what each holds and who owns it; where the project has DataHub or OpenMetadata it reads them |
| pandas and Polars | From the two projects' own documentation, with when pandas stops being enough and Polars or DuckDB take over |
| Sizing to the volume | The interview and the choice of the solution, from a small load to billions of rows, by a volume measured or estimated in writing |

### Nothing of their own

No server and no skills of their own team were found on 2026-11-15 for PostgreSQL, SQLite, Citus, Vitess, PgBouncer, Crunchy Data, Drizzle, Django, SQLMesh, Apache Airflow, Pandera, Debezium, Apache Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS, Squawk, SQLFluff, SQLGlot, OpenLineage, Marquez, tbls, SchemaSpy, Polars, pandas, Apache Spark, Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake. For all of these, rule 1 applies: the command line.

- The reference server that once served PostgreSQL and SQLite is archived: its repository says "archived by the owner on May 29, 2025" and "NO SECURITY GUARANTEES" (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers-archived).
- Oracle's MySQL server is left out by the user's decision: its page calls it "not intended for production use but as a proof of concept" (https://github.com/oracle/mcp/tree/main/src/mysql-mcp-server).
- MariaDB's earlier server is "officially deprecated" from 2026-11-03 (https://github.com/MariaDB/mcp); `mariadb-shell` succeeds it.
- Snowflake-Labs' server is deprecated, "no longer maintained" (https://github.com/Snowflake-Labs/mcp); the Snowflake-managed server succeeds it.
- Apache Flink has nothing for Flink itself; its Flink Agents project ships one skill for Flink Agents.
- Percona's one server reads Percona Monitoring and Management and no database (https://github.com/percona/pmm-mcp).
